case_name: Christian Jew Foundation v. Christian Jew Outreach
text:
COURT FILE NO.:
03-CV-249068 CM1

DATE:
May 31, 2007

ONTARIO

SUPERIOR COURT OF JUSTICE

BETWEEN:

CHRISTIAN JEW FOUNDATION and GARY HEDRICK

Plaintiffs

- and -

THE CHRISTIAN JEW OUTREACH AND ALBERT ISRAELI

Defendants

COUNSEL:

Robert W. Cosman for the Plaintiffs

Kelly L. Webster for the Defendants

HEARING DATE:
May 17, 2007

REASONS FOR DECISION

PERELL, J.

Introduction and Overview

[
1
]

The Christian Jew Outreach (“Outreach”) (which has changed its name to
The Messiah for Israel Ministries) and Mr. Albert Israeli seek leave to appeal
the terms of a costs award, and in that motion they raise the question of the
relevance of a party’s impecuniousity as a factor in the exercise of the
court’s discretion to award costs. Their motion also raises issues about the
court’s procedure for making a costs award after an interlocutory motion.

[
2
]

To be more particular, Outreach and Mr. Israeli, who are the Defendants
in this action, bring a motion for leave to appeal an award of costs made by
Master Sproat on March 5, 2007, and they ask that the court receive new
evidence on this motion. In the last regard, they delivered an affidavit from
Mr. Israeli sworn on April 25, 2007 and delivered shortly before the argument
of the motion for leave to appeal.

[
3
]

Master Sproat’s costs award was made ancillary to her decision in August
of 2006 with respect to several motions about such matters as the delivery of
further and better affidavit of documents, the production of documents, and the
validity of refusals to answer questions asked during examinations.

[
4
]

After deciding the motions, Master Sproat ordered the Defendants within
30 days to pay to the Plaintiffs’ Christian Jew Foundation (“Foundation”) and
Gary Hedrick on a partial indemnity basis the sum of $29.974.03, which is
inclusive of some disbursements, counsel fee, and GST.

[
5
]

Master Sproat reserved for the trial judge the issue of whether the
Foundation and Mr. Hedrick should recover a disbursement of $99,260.00 for the
work of a Mr. Ivor Gottschalk, a forensic accountant.

[
6
]

In seeking leave to appeal, Outreach and Mr. Israeli do not dispute the
scale or the amount of the costs award, nor do they dispute that the costs
should be payable to the Plaintiffs. Rather, they assert that the liability to
pay costs should rest only with Outreach and they object to the requirement
that the costs be paid to the Plaintiffs within 30 days. Outreach and Mr.
Israeli ask that the Master’s order be varied to order that the costs be
payable by Outreach to the Plaintiffs in any event of the cause.

[
7
]

At the heart of both the motion for leave to appeal and the request that
the Court consider new evidence is the allegation that the Defendants are
impecunious.

[
8
]

The Defendants submit that the obligation imposed on them to pay costs
within 30 days is a very serious matter because they are unable to pay and thus
are exposed to the prospect that their defence and their counterclaim will be
struck out pursuant to rule 57.03 (2), which provides that where a defendant
fails to pay costs of a motion, the court may strike out the party’s defence or
make such other order as is just. Rule 60.12 is also relevant and similar. Rule
60.12 states:

60.12   Where a party fails to comply with an interlocutory
order, the court may, in addition to any other sanction provided by these rules,

(a) stay the party’s proceeding;

(b) dismiss the party’s proceeding or strike out the
party’s defence; or

(c) make such other order as is just.

[
9
]

In their factum, they submit that “justice is subverted if [Outreach]
and Mr. Israeli never get an opportunity to go to trial.”

[
10
]

My own conclusion is that the Defendants’ motion should be dismissed. In
coming to this conclusion, I do not grant leave to appeal and I do not grant
leave to admit the new evidence but, practically speaking, I did not ignore the
new evidence, and if I had granted leave to appeal and admitted the new
evidence, I would still have dismissed the appeal on its merits and refused to
vary the costs award of Master Sproat.

[
11
]

My reasons for these conclusions, which include an analysis of the role
of impecuniousity as a factor in the court’s discretion to award costs, are set
out below. My explanation follows a brief discussion of the nature of the
claim, defence, and counterclaim in this action and of the procedural steps
that preceded Master Sproat’s costs award.

[
12
]

Before beginning the discussion and the analysis, there is one
preliminary matter to get out of the way. This matter arises because Outreach
and Mr. Israeli initially delivered a notice of motion seeking leave to appeal,
but later they also delivered a notice of appeal. In my opinion, however, there
is no appeal as of right of a master’s costs award, and the Defendants were
correct in the first instance in seeking leave to appeal.
Subsection 133
(b) of
the
Courts of Justice Act
, R.S.O. 1990, c. C.43 specifies that where a
costs order is in the discretion of the court, no appeal lies except with leave
of the court.  See M.M. Orkin,
The Law of Costs
(2
nd
ed.)
(Canada Law Book: Aurora, looseleaf), para. 801.1.

Background

[
13
]

I will begin the discussion of the background with a review of the
pleadings and some of the affidavit material filed by the parties. Since this
motion remains an interlocutory matter, I do not make any final findings of
fact.

[
14
]

The Plaintiff Foundation is a non-profit corporation under the laws of
the state of Texas, where it is recognized as a church and a charity. The
Plaintiff Mr. Hedrick lives in Texas, and he is the president of the
Foundation.

[
15
]

Mr. Hedrick was also a director of the Defendant Outreach, which is a
corporation without share capital under the laws of Canada with a head office
in Kitchener, Ontario. It also is a charity.

[
16
]

The Foundation was founded in 1948, and it has the expressed goal of
educating both Jewish and non-Jewish people about the Gospel of Jesus.

[
17
]

In or about 1993, to facilitate its relationship with donors in Canada,
the Foundation incorporated Outreach, which had similar goals to those of the
Foundation. The Defendant Mr. Israeli is a director of Outreach and a former
employee of the Foundation.

[
18
]

In or about February 1996, the Foundation hired Mr. Israeli as its
director of Russian-Jewish Ministries and he was subsequently promoted to
director of International Ministries. Mr. Israeli, who is a missionary and a
fundraiser, reported to Mr. Hedrick.

[
19
]

The Foundation’s Statement of Claim alleges that Mr. Israeli made
fraudulent representations to induce the Foundation to transfer funds to
Outreach where they could be controlled by Mr. Israeli. Amongst other purposes,
these funds were to be used for humanitarian aid; it is alleged, however, that
Mr. Israeli misappropriated the funds and breached his trust and contractual
and fiduciary duties to the Foundation. The Foundation seeks an accounting.

[
20
]

Amongst many allegations, it is alleged that Outreach has not repaid a
loan of US$323,550.00 from the Foundation. It is also alleged that Outreach and
Mr. Israeli misappropriated confidential information, committed the tort of
passing off, breached copyright, and infringed the Foundation’s trademarks. It
is alleged that Outreach has not complied with its corporate law
responsibilities and its responsibilities under the
Charities Accounting Act
,
R.S.O. 1990, c. C.10.

It is alleged that there are financial
irregularities. It is alleged that Mr. Israeli repudiated and abandoned his
employment relationship with the Foundation.

[
21
]

In their Statement of Claim, the Foundation and Mr. Hedrick claim,
amongst other things, injunctive relief of various sorts, an accounting,
damages for fraudulent misrepresentation, and damages for breach of trust in
the amount of $2,000,000.00.

[
22
]

In their Statement of Defence, Mr. Israeli and Outreach deny the
allegations made against them, and they advance a counterclaim against Mr.
Hedrick and the Foundation. Amongst many allegations, Mr. Israeli alleges: that
he was wrongfully dismissed by the Foundation; that the Foundation defamed him
and Outreach in letters sent to Outreach’s donors; and that Mr. Hedrick and the
Foundation have been unjustly enriched. Outreach and Mr. Israeli each claim $5,000,000
in general damages. Mr. Israeli claims damages of $250,000 for wrongful
dismissal. They submit that the Foundation has failed to remit to Outreach
donation proceeds owed to it.

[
23
]

Outreach and Mr. Israeli submit that the libels destroyed Outreach as a
charitable corporation and it is now dormant. They say that Mr. Israeli’s
career as a missionary and fundraiser was also destroyed and he was compelled
to find work in construction. Because of health problems, he is now unemployed.

[
24
]

The Foundation and Mr. Hedrick commenced their action in October 2002.
Mr. Israeli was examined for discovery and cross-examined on affidavit material
in the summer of 2003. Mr. Hedrick was examined for discovery in the autumn of
2003. During the examinations there were undertakings and refusals by both
sides.

[
25
]

Both sides brought motions with respect to the undertakings and
unanswered questions. These motions were heard by Master Kelly who heard
argument on May 13, 2004. The arguments, however, were not completed and Master
Kelly adjourned the motion first to July 9, 2004 and then
sine die
. (The
balance of the motion was eventually heard by Master Sproat.)

[
26
]

Meanwhile, the Foundation and Mr. Hedrick changed solicitors, and during
the period while the motions were still outstanding, they retained a forensic
accountant Mr. Ivor Gottschalk in the autumn of 2004.

[
27
]

On April 8, 2005, relying on the investigations of Mr. Gottschalk and
his affidavit, the Foundation brought a motion for a further and better
affidavit of documents from Outreach and Mr. Israeli. Mr. Israeli responded
with an affidavit of his own and cross-examinations of Mr. Gottschalk and Mr.
Israeli took place in the summer of 2005.

[
28
]

The motions for the further and better affidavit of documents and with
respect to the undertakings and unanswered questions came on before Master
Sproat on January 11, 30 and 31 and February 1, 2006. Master Sproat reserved
her decision.

[
29
]

On August 17, 2006, Master Sproat released her Endorsement and ruled,
amongst other things, that Outreach should produce financial and accounting
records. Master Sproat reserved her decision about costs and directed the
parties to make their submissions in writing.

[
30
]

The submissions of the party requesting costs were not to exceed five
pages and there was a similar limit to the responding party. Reply submissions
were not to exceed three pages. None of the parties adhered to the direction
about the page length of their costs submissions.

[
31
]

On September 7, 2006, the Foundation delivered its costs submissions. It
sought partial indemnity costs of: (a) $52,838.00 for fees for the motion for a
further and better affidavit; (b) $8,260.00 for fees for the undertakings and
refusals motion; and (c) $99,260.00 for the disbursement or expense incurred to
engage Mr. Gottschalk. In total, it sought a costs award of $177,791.35.

[
32
]

On September 22, 2006, Outreach and Mr. Israeli delivered their costs
submissions in response. They submitted that Mr. Israeli should not be
personally liable for costs. Outreach and Mr. Israeli indicated that they were
unable to pay costs of any magnitude and a costs order would deny them the
opportunity to make their case.

[
33
]

In support of their costs submissions, Outreach and Mr. Israeli provided
an affidavit from Mr. Thomas J. Corbett, who was their counsel on the motions
before Master Sproat. Mr. Corbett’s affidavit attached draft financial
statements from Outreach as of December 31, 2004. The draft financial
statements appeared to have been very recently prepared; that is, they were
dated September 20, 2006. Mr. Corbett’s affidavit indicated that Mr. Israeli
was a construction worker and that he had no significant resources to pay any
award of costs. Paragraphs 3, 4, and 6 of Mr. Corbett’s affidavit state:

Attached as Exhibit “A” is a copy of the draft financial
statements for CJO [Outreach] for December 31, 2004 provided to me by Mr.
Ahier, C.A., the accountant for CJO. Mr. Ahier advises me, and I believe that
the statement has not been done in final form.  His accounts of 2005 and 2006,
totaling $11,382 remain unpaid and he has unbilled work in progress.

I am advised by Mr. Albert Israeli and believe that the
bank accounts of CJO have very small balances, as at the August 31, 2006
statements of $1206.54 in the US account and $4595.21 in the Canadian account.

I am advised by Mr. Albert Israeli and believe that the
actions of CJF that are the subject of the counterclaim, together with the
impact of this action, has rendered CJO generally dormant pending the
conclusion of this action.  It does not have the resources to pay any award of
costs.

[
34
]

The Foundation and Mr. Hedrick then delivered an eight-page reply and
submitted that it was inappropriate for the Master to consider Mr. Corbett’s
affidavit because he was both counsel and witness in the proceeding.

[
35
]

On October 2, 2006, by letter, Outreach sought leave from the Master to
file a sur-reply. The letter objected that the Foundation and Mr. Hedrick had
split their case, and the letter addressed the Plaintiffs’ objection to the
evidence from Mr. Corbett. To address this concern, Outreach offered to deliver
an affidavit from Mr. Israeli if necessary. The same day, the Foundation wrote
the Master to object to any sur-reply.

[
36
]

Master Sproat did not reply to this correspondence and rather released
her E ndorsement about costs on March 5, 2007.

[
37
]

For present purposes, the following passages from Master Sproat’s
Endorsement are particularly relevant:

As a preliminary matter, I wish to address the filing of an
affidavit sworn by Mr. Corbett, presumably to support his submission that costs
be reserved to the trial judge on the basis of the defendants’ inability to pay
costs. I have not considered in any manner the affidavit of Mr. Corbett as it
is my view that it is highly irregular for Mr. Corbett, who appeared as counsel
on the motion and in making costs submissions, to rely on his own affidavit on
these costs submissions.  In addition, leaving aside the unfairness to the
plaintiffs by virtue of not having an opportunity to cross examine upon the
issue, the evidence is based on hearsay on a very key issue in relation to the
defendants' costs submissions.

In the event that I had erred in refusing to consider this
affidavit evidence, I would have given very little weight to the evidence in
view of the failure to produce the best evidence (i.e. of Mr. Israeli or
Christian and Jew Outreach) and the lack of evidence as to the relationship
between the Messiah for Israel Ministries Inc. (the "Messiah") and
the defendants.  I further observed that the financial statements are draft and
unsigned by a representative of the Messiah.  Lastly, it appeared to me that
the financial statements appeared to have been prepared for the specific
purpose of the costs submissions, the same being dated one day prior to Mr.
Corbett’s swearing of the affidavit.  I find the latter peculiar in view of the
outdated nature of the financial information, being in the year ended 2004. . .
. .

I do not accept that costs ought to be reserved to the
trial judge.  The rules require that costs of motions be fixed and payable
within 30 days, for the reasons that the motions master or judge, as the case
may be, is in the best position to fix costs.  In addition, it is my view that
there must be some sanction for failing to consider the merits of a motion and
unnecessary opposition to a motion.  In my view, there is no reason why the
plaintiffs ought to be out of pocket in relation to these hard fought motions.

I do not accept that the defendants are unable to pay
costs, for the reasons stated above, with respect to Mr. Corbett’s affidavit.

Lastly, I would observe that the defendants have launched a
counterclaim for an amount far in excess of what is claimed by the plaintiffs.
The court does not accept that the costs of the motions ought to be deferred
when the defendants are not merely "defendants", but rather have
asserted a counterclaim.  . . . .

As to the disbursements, I have no difficulties with the
disbursements claimed by the plaintiffs, save the $100,000 claimed for the
forensic investigation conducted by Gottschalk.  While Gottschalk’s evidence
with respect to the need for additional documents was filed on the motion, it
is my view that this disbursement is properly left to be considered upon the
disposition of the action given Gottschalk’s likely broader involvement in the
litigation.  I decline to award the Gottschalk disbursement without prejudice
to the right of the plaintiffs to seek recovery of this amount in the cause.
All other disbursements are reasonable and in my view, properly claimed by the
plaintiffs.

[
38
]

As already noted in the introduction, Outreach and Mr. Israeli now seek
leave to appeal from the costs award of Master Sproat and they also seek leave
to adduce the affidavit of Mr. Israeli.

[
39
]

Mr. Israeli’s late arriving affidavit is virtually identical to the
affidavit of Mr. Corbett that was rejected by Master Sproat.

Discussion and Analysis

[
40
]

The test for granting leave to appeal of a discretionary costs award is
set out in
Rona Inc. v. Sevenbridge Developments Ltd.
,
[2002] O.J. No.
3938 (S.C.J.)
. There are four elements: (a) the applicant must identify a good
arguable case having enough merit to warrant the scrutiny of the court; (b) the
issues must be important both to the parties and in general; (c) the appeal
must have practical utility; and (d) the court should consider the effect of
the delay in proceedings caused by the appeal. For the purposes of deciding
this motion, the critical element is whether Outreach and Mr. Israeli have an
arguable case having enough merit to warrant the scrutiny of the court.

[
41
]

On an appeal from a master's order that is a matter of discretion, the
court will only interfere if the master was clearly wrong or if he or she
exercised discretion based on wrong principles or under a misapprehension of
the facts:
Bank of Nova Scotia v. Liberty Mutual Insurance Co.
(2003),

2003 CanLII 35171 (ON SCDC)
, 67 O.R. (3d) 699 (Div. Ct.);
Marleen Investments Ltd. v. McBride
(1979),

1979 CanLII 1895 (ON HCJ)
, 23 O.R. (2d) 125 (H.C.J.);
Woodheath Developments Ltd. v. Goldman

(2003),
2003 CanLII 46735 (ON SCDC)
, 66 O.R. (3d) 731 (Div. Ct.);
Fotwe v. Citadel General Assurance Co.,

2005 CanLII 5470 (ON SCDC)
, [2005] O.J. No. 827 (Div. Ct.).

[
42
]

An appellate court should defer to the findings of fact of a motions
judge or master unless the judge or master disregarded or failed to appreciate
relevant evidence:
Bottan v. Vroom
,
[2002] O.J. No. 1383 (C.A.)
.

[
43
]

Outreach and Mr. Israeli argue that the Master erred in law and in
principle. As I understand their argument, they essentially advance five
grounds for leave to appeal and as justification for varying the order of
Master Sproat; namely they argue that: (a) Master Sproat erred by awarding
costs against Mr. Israeli personally; (b) she erred in her treatment of the
evidence of the Defendants’ impecuniousity by rejecting or discounting Mr.
Corbett’s affidavit, which they submit was not even necessary to put the evidence
of impecuniousity before the court; (c) alternatively, she erred in not
allowing (by a sur-reply) a replacement affidavit from Mr. Israeli to be filed;
(d) she made her award under a misapprehension of facts, wrongly concluding
that the Defendants were not impecunious; and (e) she did not properly exercise
her discretion having regard to the Defendants’ impecuniousity and the effect
of the order on the Defendants’ ability to have their day in court.

[
44
]

I can be very brief about the first ground for leave to appeal. In my
opinion, there is no merit to the Defendants’ argument that costs should only
be awarded against Outreach and not against Mr. Israeli. Master Sproat made no
error in principle in arriving at her conclusion. Mr. Israeli is a party to the
action and counterclaim, and he was an active contestant in what turned out
from his perspective to be a largely unsuccessful series of interlocutory
motions. In my opinion, the Master was correct in deciding that Mr. Israeli
should be liable for costs.

[
45
]

The other grounds for leave to appeal or as justification to vary Master
Sproat’s costs award, which overlap one another, are more substantial.

[
46
]

The role of costs and the procedural means to have them assessed are
problematic, and there is no doubt that in recent years, the administrators of
justice, including judges, masters, registrars, assessment officers, the
Ministry of the Attorney General, the Civil Rules Committee, and even local bar
associations and professional organizations have experimented and suggested
ways to fairly and efficiently adjudicate claims for costs, which can be very
substantial and even can grow to be more important than the claims and
defences. There are significant policy issues, legal issues that can rise to
the level of constitutional law controversies, and human resource issues
associated with the assessment of costs. Generally speaking, the contemporary
approach involves some formal and informal elements. The
Courts of Justice
Act

and the
Rules of Civil Procedure
provide some guidance, but
judges and masters exercise some discretion as to the procedure to follow.

[
47
]

It is in this context that Master Sproat adopted a conventional and a
contemporary approach to the assessment of costs. She directed the parties to
make submissions to her in writing. In my opinion, the approach adopted by
Master Sproat was appropriate and it was not suggested that her general
approach manifested an error in principle. She seems to have modeled her
directions about written costs submissions after the classical model of a trial
or motion where the claimant puts in a case, the respondent puts in a case, and
the claimant puts in a reply without splitting his or her case. This approach
satisfies the requirements of natural justice and recognizes that there must be
rules of evidence and procedure, including a way to end the adjudication.

[
48
]

In the case at bar, Outreach and Mr. Israeli decided to raise the issue
of their own impecuniousity as part of their case about costs. To provide
evidence of impecuniousity, they relied on the affidavit of Mr. Corbett to
which an objection was taken by the Foundation and Mr. Hedrick on the ground
that Mr. Corbett was both counsel and witness and therefore this evidence
should be rejected.

[
49
]

Ultimately, as I read her Reasons for Decision, Master Sproat rejected
Mr. Corbett’s evidence on the ground that he should not be witness and counsel
and on the alternatively ground that she was not persuaded by his hearsay
evidence. To my mind, the alternative ground for her treatment of the evidence
was the determinative and the more important ground to conclude that the case
for impecuniousity had not been proven by Outreach and Mr. Israeli.

[
50
]

Assuming for the sake of argument that Master Sproat should not have
rejected Mr. Corbett’s affidavit outright, a point to which I will return, she
gave good reasons for rejecting his evidence as hearsay and perhaps double
hearsay having regard to the fact that the accountant prepared the financial
statements based on information that he heard from others.

[
51
]

Having regard to the nature of the litigation itself, which involves
competing allegations of failure to account for funds, there was good reason
for Master Sproat to be cautious in accepting this evidence of impecuniousity.
She cannot be said to have made an error in principle in rejecting this
evidence. If she made an error, and I do not think that she did, it was an
error in a finding of fact, and this is the kind of error for which she is
entitled to deference from an appellate court.

[
52
]

Outreach and Mr. Israeli submitted that costs submissions are usually
made without any formal evidentiary proof and Mr. Corbett’s providing his own
affidavit is actually more formal than the evidentiary informality of
submissions about costs made by counsel after a hearing and relied on by the
court. There is strength to this submission, because it is true that costs
submissions have historically often been made informally:
Andrews v. Andrews
,

[1983] O.J. No. 456 (H.C.J.)
. However, this submission does not go far enough to
justify overturning the costs award of Master Sproat because, even if no
objection can be taken to the evidence being submitted by counsel’s affidavit,
it remained for the Master to weigh the evidence and decide whether or not
impecuniousity was proven.

[
53
]

The Foundation and Mr. Hedrick submitted that Mr. Corbett’s affidavit
should be rejected categorically. The rule of professional conduct in Ontario,
however, is not categorical. Rule 4.02 (1) of the
Rules of Professional
Conduct
states: “Subject to any contrary provisions of the law or the
discretion of the tribunal before which a lawyer is appearing, a lawyer who
appears as advocate shall not submit his or her own affidavit to the tribunal.”
As I note in
Conflicts of Interest in the Legal Profession
(Butterworths:
Markham, 1995) at p. 78-79, where I cite the voluminous authority on the point:
“Case law establishes that when a lawyer is a witness in person, a deponent by
affidavit, or the source of information in another person’s affidavit sworn on
information and belief, it is extremely undesirable for the lawyer to act or to
continue to act as counsel before the tribunal, although the practice is not
absolutely prohibited and the evidence is admissible.”

[
54
]

In the end result, Master Sproat, as she was entitled to be, was not
satisfied that impecuniousity had been proven, and it follows that she did not
need to consider and cannot be faulted for not considering impecuniousity as a
factor in the exercise of her discretion about costs. Moreover, she did not err
in not permitting a sur-reply to allow more evidence of impecuniousity to be
tendered. Outreach and Mr. Israeli, perhaps for tactical, strategic, practical,
or pragmatic reasons, had decided how it would advance this point and from a
due process point of view, it had been given its opportunity to be heard.

[
55
]

For similar reasons, I would reject the submission of Mr. Israeli’s
affidavit as evidence on the leave to appeal motion. In my view, it suffers
from the same frailties as submissions from Mr. Corbett, be they informal or
sworn in an affidavit. The evidence is largely hearsay, it is self-serving, it
wants for testing by cross-examination, and frankly its probative value is
unclear.

[
56
]

These conclusions are sufficient to explain why I am dismissing this
motion for leave to appeal, and I need not go on to consider the argument that
Master Sproat did not properly exercise her discretion having regard to the
Defendants’ impecuniousity and the effect of the order on the Defendants’
ability to have their day in court.

[
57
]

However, in fairness to the arguments of both parties, I think I should
address the role of impecuniosity as a factor in the court’s discretion to make
and enforce a costs award.

Impecuniousity as a Factor in the Court’s Discretion to
Make and Enforce a Costs Award

[
58
]

For a motion, subrule 57.03 (1) directs that costs be fixed and made
payable within 30 days; however, the subrule contains the phrase “unless the
court is satisfied that a different order would be more just.” Thus, the court
may depart from the general principle that costs are payable within 30 days;
for example, by ordering costs in the cause or by reserving the issue of costs
to the trial judge:
Giang v. Le
,
2004 CanLII 5036 (ON SC)
, [2004] O.J. No. 569 (S.C.J.). For the
case before me, the general question is what role, if any, should a party’s
impecuniousity play in the exercise of the court’s discretion when making and
enforcing costs awards.

[
59
]

Before addressing the role of impecuniousity as it pertains to costs
awards, it may be said that in the immediate case notwithstanding Master
Sproat’s conclusion that impecuniousity was not proven, she seems to have not
totally ignored the factor. Her conclusion that the disbursement of Mr.
Gottschalk should be referred to the trial judge shows sensitivity to the
possibly oppressive nature of a costs award that is made immediately payable
and her award of $25,000 (net of GST) for counsel fee was a reduction from a
claim of approximately $61,000 (net of GST) shows a similar sensitivity.

[
60
]

In any event, because of her finding of fact, ultimately Master Sproat
did not treat impecuniousity as a relevant factor in the exercise of her
discretion with respect to costs and I will explore whether this leads to a
reversal error in the circumstances of this case.

[
61
]

I begin this exploration by noting that there are authorities that
support the proposition that a party’s impecuniousity is not a relevant factor
in the exercise of a court’s discretion in awarding or enforcing costs awards.
In particular, impecuniousity will not insulate a party from liability of costs
otherwise payable and impecuniousity cannot be used as a justification for
failure to obey a court orders:
Meyers v. Marks
,
1995 CanLII 11086 (ON CTGDDC)
, [1995] O.J. No. 1321
(Div. Ct.);
Abbott v. Reuter-Stokes Canada Ltd.
(1988), 32 C.P.C. (2d)
161 (Ont. L.J.S.C.)
;
Stacey v. Barrie Yacht Club
,
[2003] O.J. No. 4171
(S.C.J.)
;
Baksh v. Sun Media (Toronto) Corp.
(2003),
2003 CanLII 64288 (ON SC)
, 63 O.R. (3d) 51
(Master);
Heu v. Forder Estate
,
[2004] O.J. No. 705 (Master)
;
Scavarelli
v. Bank of Montreal¸
[2004] O.J. No. 2175 (S.C.J.)
;
Cossette v. Gojit
(Brampton Inc.)
,
[2005] O.J. No. 6098 (Master)
;
Kirwin v. Silver Brooke
Golf Course Inc.
,
[2006] O.J. No. 1571 (S.C.J.)
.

[
62
]

The policy rationales behind this line of authority are that: (a) a rule
based on impecuniousity would present problems of interpretation, evidence, and
application and such a rule would be undesirable; (b) and the courts would
become powerless to control an impecunious party who could bring and defend
motions without fear of any sanction for irresponsibly bringing or resisting interlocutory
motions, and, therefore, impecuniousity should not be a factor in awarding or
enforcing costs awards.

[
63
]

If this line of authority applies to the case at bar, Master Sproat
cannot be faulted for failing to consider the impecuniousity of Outreach and
Mr. Israeli as a factor in the exercise of her discretion.

[
64
]

There are, however, authorities that support the proposition that
impecuniosity is a relevant factor and may be considered in awarding and in
enforcing costs awards including determining when the costs should be payable:
Larabie
v. Montfils
(2004),
2004 CanLII 11299 (ON CA)
, 44 C.P.C. (5
th
) 66 (Ont. C.A.);
J.S.
Saville Holdings Inc. v. Suzuki Canada Inc.
,
[1995] O.J. No. 3758 (Gen.
Div.)
;
Tanner v. Clark
,
2002 CanLII 34779 (ON SCDC)
, [2002] O.J. No. 3702 (Div. Ct.), affd. (2003),

2003 CanLII 41640 (ON CA)
, 63 O.R. (3d) 508 (C.A.);
Coombs (Litigation Guardian of) v. ACE INA
Insurance,
[2004] O.J. No. 3788 (S.C.J.)
;
Leo A. Seydel Ltd.(c.o.b.
Canadian Tire Associate Store No. 126) v. Francis
,
[2005] O.J. No. 706
(S.C.J.)
.

[
65
]

The policy rationale behind this competing line of cases that access to
justice is a necessary and desirable attribute of the administration of justice
and access to justice may be thwarted if the effect of a party’s impecuniousity
is ignored when the court exercises its discretion to award or enforce a costs award.

[
66
]

Perhaps the strongest case in this line of authorities is the judgment
of Blair, J.A. sitting in chambers for the Court of Appeal in
Larabie v.
Montfils
(2004),
2004 CanLII 11299 (ON CA)
, 44 C.P.C. (5
th
) 66 (Ont. C.A.). In this case,
Mr. Larabie had an action struck out as an abuse of process principally because
he had in earlier proceedings advanced a similar claim. Mr. Larabie appealed
the dismissal of his action, and the respondents sought security for costs and
they also sought an order staying the action, including Mr. Larabie’s appeal,
because of the non-payment of costs orders already made against Mr. Larabie.

[
67
]

Mr. Larabie pleaded impecuniosity and although Justice Blair was
obviously troubled by whether he should give weight to this factor, he decided
that justice demanded that Mr. Larabie’s appeal proceed notwithstanding his
non-compliance with the orders of the court. Justice Blair stated in paragraphs
13 to 18 and 21 of his Reasons for Decision:

13

Here,
there is no doubt that Mr. Larabie has not paid numerous outstanding orders for
costs against him, in significant amounts; that he is a non-resident of
Ontario; and that his has insufficient assets in Ontario to pay those costs or
the costs of the pending appeal. There is ample basis upon which the court
could exercise its discretion both to stay the action and to order security for
costs on the appeal.

14

Mr.
Larabie has caused the defendants to respond to the various proceedings outlined
above, in all of which he has been unsuccessful, and has refused to pay any of
the outstanding costs orders against him. Now he has commenced a new action,
making the very same allegations as those in the proceeding in which the courts
have already ruled against him. That action has been dismissed, with costs
(also unpaid) and Mr. Larabie has appealed to the Court of Appeal. The moving
parties submit that the court should exercise its discretion under the
foregoing rules and stay the action until Mr. Larabie has paid the outstanding
costs and, further, order that he provide security for costs of the appeal.

15

Although
the decision is not an easy one, I am not prepared to do so, for the following
reasons.

16

I
am satisfied on the record that Mr. Larabie is an impecunious plaintiff. His
income is limited to approximately $840 per month in the form of a disability
pension from the Federal Government and he becomes eligible for the old age
pension this month. He has no assets save for basic clothing and a few personal
belongings. He simply has no means of satisfying the outstanding costs orders
or of posting any meaningful amount as security for costs. To accede to the
moving parties' requests would end the proceedings for all practical purposes
and, in effect, bar him from the judicial process without him having had a
final chance to persuade the court that he should be permitted to have his
claims adjudicated on the merits.

17

There
is ample authority for the proposition that the courts are reluctant to deprive
a worthy but impecunious litigant of the opportunity to have his or her claim
adjudicated when it is not plainly devoid of merit: see, for example,
Rackley
v. Rice
(1992),
1992 CanLII 7717 (ON CTGD)
, 8 O.R. (3d) 105 (Ont. Div. Ct.);
John Wink Ltd. v. Sico
Inco
(1987),
1987 CanLII 4299 (ON HCJ)
, 57 O.R. (2d) 705 (Ont. H.C.);
Solcan Electric Corp. v.
Viewstar Canada Inc.

(1994), 25 C.P.C. (3d) 181 (Ont. Gen. Div.)
;
1056470
Ontario Inc. v. Choo-Eng Goh
(1997),
1997 CanLII 12255 (ON CTGD)
, 34 O.R. (3d) 92. Although these are
lower court decisions the same principle should apply in appeals in this court,
in my view.

18

The problem here is that Mr. Larabie has
never had the opportunity to have his case considered on the merits. In
hindsight, of course, it might have been better if the original order of Manton
J. had been appealed. When that was not done the substance of his claim were
overshadowed by procedural questions as to whether or not the matter had become

res judicata
and thereafter whether the various requisites for appeal or
leave to appeal had been met.

21

I am not unmindful of the moving parties'
arguments outlined above, nor am I unsympathetic towards the position in which
they find themselves. Litigants are not free to ignore or flout orders of the
court awarding costs against them or to re-litigate matters that have truly
been litigated and decided before. Having considered all of the circumstances,
however, and having weighed and balanced the various competing interests and
factors in relation to this matter, I conclude that I should exercise my
discretion in favour of permitting Mr. Larabie to proceed with the appeal, and
to do so without having to post security for costs. I expect that he will do so
in a reasonably expeditious fashion.

[
68
]

In this passage, Justice Blair refers to the jurisprudence associated
with a motion for security for costs where the court will permit an impecunious
plaintiff to litigate without posting security for costs out of concerns that
access to justice not be denied. Justice Blair’s Reasons, however, are not
limited to motions for security for costs and he addresses the problem of a
party relying on poverty as a means to insulate himself or herself from
compliance with court orders. Ultimately, Justice Blair refuses to adopt a
categorical approach and leaves the court with some discretion to recognize
impecuniousity as a factor in the exercise of its discretion in ordering
security for costs and in making and enforcing costs awards.

[
69
]

In my opinion, Justice Blair’s approach is both the one I must follow
and also the preferable approach. In most cases, impecuniousity will not be a
factor; however, as I understand Justice Blair’s more flexible approach, in the
exercise of its discretion, a court can probe the circumstances and assess,
what might be called “the procedural good faith” of the party using
impecuniousity as his or her excuse for failing to comply with a court order,
including a failure to pay costs. Is the person using impeciousity as a means
to avoid his or her responsibilities or in good faith as an apology or
explanation for failing to do so?

[
70
]

I note that Master Dash, who is a proponent of the more rigid approach
that would not treat impecuniousity as a relevant criterion, left room for
exceptional cases. In
Heu v. Forder Estate
,
supra
at p. 22 he
stated: “There may be situations where a clearly meritorious case should not be
dismissed against an impecunious plaintiff for failing to pay interlocutory
costs orders, but given the need of the court to retain control over its
process and the legitimacy of its orders, such situations should be the
exception and not the norm.”

[
71
]

Because of the factual finding in the case at bar that impecuniousity
was not proven, it was not necessary for Master Sproat to exercise her
discretion. Nevertheless, in my opinion, had impecuniousity been proven and had
Master Sproat exercised her discretion to require Outreach and Mr. Israeli to
pay costs within 30 days this would not have been clearly wrong.

[
72
]

Further, it remains to be seen whether the Foundation and Mr. Hedrick
will move and rely on rules 57.03 (2) or 60.12 to stay the counterclaim or
strike out the party’s defence; in that event, following
Larabie v. Montfils
,

supra
, the court retains the discretion to permit the defence and
counterclaim to proceed.

[
73
]

Therefore, I conclude that the ground of appeal based on the role of
impecuniosity as a factor in the court’s discretion to make and enforce a costs
award is also not made out.

Conclusion

[
74
]

For these reasons, I conclude that this motion for leave to appeal
should be dismissed.

[
75
]
